title: Morality, sexuality and the church's record
intro:
Some of these pages concern harm done to people who are still alive, abuse in churches above all. For anyone who has been harmed, Find Help (/help) lists places to turn now, and a crime against a child or anyone else is reported to the police, whatever a church says. Nothing here asks a person who has been hurt to stay silent, and nothing here is offered as an excuse for what was done.

The case against Christianity that most people meet first is not an argument about God. It is the record of Christians. The Crusades were preached by popes. Catholic and Protestant authorities burned and drowned people for their beliefs, and some of the church's greatest teachers wrote the arguments that justified it. Christian nations built the Atlantic slave trade and the conquest of the Americas, and churches defended both from the Bible. Church leaders hid the abuse of children to protect their institutions. Critics from David Hume and Thomas Paine to Christopher Hitchens have pressed this record against the faith itself.

These pages begin there, with the church's record, and they concede its guilt first and plainly. The church named here is not someone else's church: Catholics and Protestants alike stand inside the record, and where a particular church body is named, it is named as a matter of history. Each page then asks what the record shows. It sets out the evidence from sources that can be checked, gives numbers only where a source gives them and says how uncertain they are, and refuses the defense that someone else did worse. Where the history corrects a false claim, the page says so and says that the correction lessens nothing. And each asks whether the wrongs were the faith's own logic or a betrayal of it, judged by the teaching of Jesus and by the Christians who opposed them from inside the church.

Pages on morality itself and on sexuality, which the plan also places in this area, are still to be written.

pieces.question: Weren't the Crusades a holy war of conquest, and don't they show what Christianity does when it has power?
pieces.blurb: Hume's verdict, the preaching at Clermont and the promise of forgiveness, the massacres of 1096 and 1099 and the sack of Constantinople, the conquests that came before, and the cross made a soldier's badge.

pieces.question: Christians tortured and burned people for what they believed. How can a faith that ran the Inquisition claim to be good?
pieces.blurb: Paine's charge, Augustine's turn and Aquinas's argument for death, the Spanish Inquisition and the *conversos*, the Protestant executions in Zurich and Geneva, the early church's refusal of force, and the case for liberty made from inside the faith.

pieces.question: Christian nations conquered the Americas and built the Atlantic slave trade, and their churches blessed both. Doesn't that discredit the faith they claimed?
pieces.blurb: Douglass and Las Casas as witnesses, the papal grants of conquest and enslavement, the Southern Baptist Convention's founding in 1845 and its apology in 1995, what the Bible says of kidnapping and of one human family, and who first resisted.

pieces.question: Church leaders hid the sexual abuse of children and protected the abusers. How can anyone trust a church, or the faith it preaches, after that?
pieces.blurb: The Catholic studies of 2004 and the Southern Baptist report of 2022, the pattern of the cover-up, what Scripture says of shepherds who feed on the flock, why abuse is reported to the police, and what makes a church safe; it gives no legal advice and asks no one to trust, return or forgive. Find Help (/help) and the police are at the top of the page and at its end.

pieces.question: Christopher Hitchens said that religion poisons everything. Hasn't religion caused more wars and cruelty than anything else in history?
pieces.blurb: The New Atheists' charge and Paine's, the French wars of religion and the Thirty Years' War, what those wars were also about, Paine's own witness to the revolutionary tribunals, and idolatry under any banner.

pieces.question: What does the Bible say about homosexuality, and why do Christians disagree?
pieces.blurb: The six passages read closely with their debated words, the historic teaching of the church and the newer reading, each in its holders' terms, where each side says the other goes wrong, and what all should confess; the page takes no side, and Find Help is named at its start and its end.

pieces.question: The Bible never mentions abortion. What did the first Christians believe about it, and about leaving unwanted infants to die?
pieces.blurb: Exposure and abortion in the Roman world, the Jewish refusal, the Didache, Barnabas, Athenagoras, Tertullian and Basil in their own words, Exodus 21:22 in both readings, and how Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Christians have reasoned; history and theology, not an argument about any law. It opens and closes with a word of gentleness for anyone carrying grief or guilt, and names Find Help.

pieces.question: The Bible tells wives to submit and women to keep silent, and the church kept women down for centuries. Is Christianity bad for women?
pieces.blurb: Stanton's charge and the texts behind it, Tertullian and Aquinas in their own words, what Jesus and the first churches did, the household codes read whole, the complementarian and egalitarian readings without a side taken, and the misuse of submission named and refused; Find Help is named for anyone being hurt.

pieces.question: Every nation's laws rest on somebody's morals. Why shouldn't a Christian people want a Christian nation? Is Christian nationalism Christian?
pieces.blurb: The case for a Christian nation in its defenders' terms, what is true in it, what Jesus did with power, the church under Constantine and after, the wars of religion, the dissenters who argued for liberty of conscience, and the same test applied to any cause that drafts the cross.

pieces.question: Morals differ from one culture to the next, and Nietzsche traced Christian values to the resentment of the weak. Isn't Christian morality just the product of its culture?
pieces.blurb: Relativism and Nietzsche's genealogy at full strength, where Christian ethics cut against the world that first heard it (unwanted infants, the poor, human rank, enemies) and later against Christian societies on slavery, with the church's guilt admitted, and what an argument from history can and can't show.

words.meaning: a war preached by the medieval church as an act of devotion, whose fighters took the cross as their sign and were promised forgiveness of sins.
the hiding of a wrong, here the abuse of children, to protect a person or an institution from its consequences.
the teaching, by a baptized person, of what the church holds to contradict the faith.
a church tribunal for finding and judging heresy; the Spanish Inquisition, founded in 1478 under the crown, was abolished in 1834.
a Jew, or a descendant of Jews, baptized in medieval Spain, often under pressure.
a North African church that broke with the catholic bishops after the persecution under Diocletian, and was suppressed by imperial law from 405.
the wars fought in Europe between Catholics and Protestants after the Reformation, among them the French civil wars of 1562 to 1598 and the Thirty Years' War of 1618 to 1648.
the error of making the cross the badge of a people's power, so that its enemies are treated as God's enemies and devotion is measured by willingness to fight.
